--- format: revealjs-clean: css: misc/slides.css --- # Raster Operations
Map algebra {.r-fit-text .titlepage} ## Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson you will be able to: - Explain the four sensor **resolution types** and their trade-offs - Distinguish and apply the four **map algebra operation types** in R - Understand why **spectral indices** are more robust than raw band values - Perform **raster–vector operations**: crop, mask, and extract - Connect **focal operations** to convolutions in image processing # Sensor Concepts {.titlepage} ## The Four Resolutions 1. **Spatial**: Ground size of one pixel 2. **Temporal**: Revisit frequency 3. **Spectral**: Number & width of bands 4. **Radiometric**: Intensity levels (bit depth) **Trade-off example:** Sentinel-2: 10 m · 5 days · 13 bands vs. MODIS: 500 m · daily · 36 bands — higher resolution in one dimension typically comes at the cost of another. ::: {.notes} - Flood mapping needs daily updates → MODIS; field-level crop mapping needs 10 m pixels → Sentinel-2 - Hyperspectral sensors (EnMAP, AVIRIS) trade spatial resolution for hundreds of spectral bands - Radiometric resolution: 16-bit captures far more detail than 8-bit ::: ## From Sensor to Analysis{.smaller} **DN vs. Reflectance** - Sensors record **Digital Numbers (DN)**: raw detector output - DN values depend on illumination angle, atmospheric conditions, and sensor calibration — **not directly comparable** across dates or sensors **Calibration pipeline:** | Step | Corrects for | |------|-------------| | DN → Radiance | Sensor gain & offset | | Radiance → TOA Reflectance | Solar illumination angle | | TOA → Surface Reflectance | Atmospheric scattering & absorption | Spectral indices are designed to work with reflectance: more **sensor- and date-independent** than raw DN. ::: {.notes} - Sentinel-2 Level-2A = surface reflectance (scaled ×10 000); Level-1C = TOA only — always check the product level - Computing NDVI on raw Level-2A integers still gives the right *ratio* (the scale cancels), but matters when comparing across sensors - How each step works: - DN → Radiance: per-band gain/offset scaling - Radiance → TOA Reflectance: normalise by solar irradiance & zenith angle - TOA → Surface Reflectance: radiative transfer model (e.g. Sen2Cor) ::: # Map Algebra {.titlepage} ## Introduction - Map algebra: operations that modify or summarize raster cell values - Four subclasses, differing in **spatial scope**: 1. **Local** — per-cell operations 2. **Focal** — central cell + neighborhood (typically 3×3) 3. **Zonal** — irregular regions defined by a second raster 4. **Global** — entire raster(s) ::: {.notes} - The four types differ in **spatial scope** — how many cells contribute to each output value - Which type gives mean elevation per municipality? Which smooths noise in an image? ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Operation Types — Illustrated ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Local (one cell), Focal (3×3 neighborhood), Zonal (coloured regions), Global (entire raster)](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-op-types-1.png){#fig-op-types width=960} ::: ::: ## Global Operation (1) - The most common global operations are descriptive statistics for the entire raster dataset such as the minimum, maximum or mean value. - For example: What is the mean elevation value for Luxembourg? ::: {.notes} - Common mistake: `mean(r)` computes a per-cell mean across bands (a **local** operation) — use `global()` for raster-wide statistics ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Elevation of Luxembourg](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-elev-1.png){#fig-elev width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # note: mean(r) does not work, since "mean" is used as a local operator mean_elev <- global(r, mean, na.rm = TRUE) mean_elev ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean elevation 348.3366 ``` ::: ::: ## Global Operation (2) - Another type of "global" operation is `distance` - This function calculates the distance from each cell to a specific target cell - For example, what is the distance from each cell to *Luxembourg City*, the capital of Luxembourg? ::: {.notes} - Why global, not local? A local operation uses only the value at (i,j) to produce the output at (i,j). Distance requires knowledge of the entire raster's spatial extent and cell coordinates — no cell can be computed in isolation. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r_dist <- distance(r, luxembourg_city) r_dist <- mask(r_dist, r) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - `distance()` computes straight-line (Euclidean) distance — not travel distance along roads or terrain. - Resistance can be incorporated via a **cost-distance** approach: supply a friction/resistance raster (e.g. slope, land cover) and use `terra::costDist()` to accumulate cost along the least-cost path. This is common in habitat connectivity and accessibility analysis. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Zonal - Zonal operations apply an aggregation function to multiple raster cells - A second raster with categorical values define the "zones" What is the mean altitude *per municipality*? ::: {.notes} - Conceptually: spatial `group_by` + `summarize` - The zones raster must be integer/categorical — use `rasterize()` to convert vector polygons first ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean_vals <- zonal(r, zones, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Zonal — Result ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-zonal-1.png){#fig-zonal width=960} ::: ::: :::{.notes} - The global operation can be seen as a special case of a zonal operation, where the only "Zone" is the entire dataset ::: ## Local (1) - Local operations comprise all cell-by-cell operations in one or several layers. - For example, we can classify the elevation into values above and below a certain threshold ::: {.notes} - All arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`) and logical (`>`, `<`, `&`, `|`) operators work element-wise on rasters in terra - Boolean rasters are the foundation of masking and multi-condition selection (e.g. the solar panel task) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # first, create a boolean copy of the raster r_bool <- as.logical(r) mean_elev <- as.numeric(mean_elev) mean_elev ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 348.3366 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} r_bool[r > mean_elev] <- FALSE r_bool[r <= mean_elev] <- TRUE ``` ::: ## Local (1) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Local (2) - This type of (re-) classification is a very common operation - For more than 2 categories, we can use `classify` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cuts <- global(r, quantile, probs = c(0, .33, .66, 1), na.rm = TRUE) r_classify <- classify(r, as.numeric(cuts)) # this next line just replaces the default labels with some custom ones levels(r_classify) <- data.frame(ID = 0:2, category = c("low","mid","high")) ``` ::: ## Local (2) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Local (3) {.smaller} - Local operations are often used with multiple bands - For example, we could calculate the mean intensity values of red, green and blue: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} l7 <- rast(system.file("tif/L7_ETMs.tif",package = "stars")) names(l7) <- c("B", "G", "R", "NIR", "SWIR", "MIR") l7_rgb <- l7[[c("R","G", "B")]] plot(l7_rgb, nr = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Local (3) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} l7_rgb_mean <- mean(l7_rgb) plot(l7_rgb_mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Local (4) {.smaller} - Local operations also work across bands — each output cell combines values from multiple input layers - For example, **weighted brightness** emphasises red over green and blue: $$B = 0.5 \times R + 0.3 \times G + 0.2 \times B$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brightness <- 0.5 * l7[["R"]] + 0.3 * l7[["G"]] + 0.2 * l7[["B"]] ``` ::: ## Local (4) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Spectral Indices {.titlepage} ::: {.notes} - Transition: we just saw that local operations can combine bands with arbitrary weights — spectral indices are exactly that, but the weights and formula are chosen to highlight a specific physical property of the surface. The weighted brightness example was arbitrary; spectral indices are grounded in how materials interact with light. ::: ## Spectral Indices: Why They Work {.smaller} Healthy vegetation has a characteristic spectral signature: - **Absorbs red** (~650 nm): chlorophyll uses it for photosynthesis - **Strongly reflects NIR** (~800 nm): leaf cell structure scatters infrared light ::: {.notes} - Why not just use NIR alone? NIR is not unique to vegetation — bare soil, sand, and snow also have moderate-to-high NIR reflectance. What is unique to healthy vegetation is **high NIR combined with low Red**. NDVI exploits this contrast: a sandy surface has high NIR *and* high Red → NDVI ≈ 0; healthy vegetation has high NIR but low Red → NDVI close to 1. The normalization by (NIR + Red) also reduces the influence of varying illumination and atmospheric haze. ::: ![Numbers indicate Landsat TM bands: 1 Blue, 2 Green, 3 Red, 4 NIR, 5 SWIR1, 7 SWIR2 (band 6 thermal, off-chart). Source: [seos-project.eu](https://seos-project.eu/remotesensing/remotesensing-c01-p06.html)](img/Reflexionskurven.jpg) ## Normalized Difference Indices $$\text{Index} = \frac{A - B}{A + B} \in [-1,\, +1]$$ Normalization reduces the effect of illumination differences. | Index | Formula | Detects | |-------|---------|---------| | **NDVI** | (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red) | Vegetation density | | **NDWI** | (Green − NIR) / (Green + NIR) | Open water | | **NDSI** | (Green − SWIR) / (Green + SWIR) | Snow & ice | | **NBR** | (NIR − SWIR) / (NIR + SWIR) | Burn severity | ::: {.notes} - All are **local raster operations** — same cell-by-cell arithmetic, different band combinations - Normalization cancels much of the multiplicative effect of illumination - NDWI has two conflicting definitions: Gao (1996) uses NIR/SWIR; McFeeters (1996) uses Green/NIR — always check which is cited - NBR is widely used for post-fire damage assessment with Sentinel-2 or Landsat ::: # Focal Operations {.titlepage} ## Focal {#sec-focal-1} - While local functions operate on one cell focal operations take into account a central (focal) cell *and its neighbors*. - The neighborhood (also named kernel, filter or moving window) under consideration is typically of size 3-by-3 cells (that is the central cell and its eight surrounding neighbors), but can take on any other size or shape as defined by the user. - A focal operation applies an aggregation function to all cells within the specified neighborhood, uses the corresponding output as the new value for the central cell, and moves on to the next central cell ::: {.notes} - Key trade-off: larger window → more smoothing but larger NA border (edge effect) - `fillNA = TRUE` mitigates this by using whatever neighbors are available at the edges ::: :::{#fig-focal} ![](img/focal.png) Note how, depending on the size of your moving window, NA's are produced. Source: @lovelace2019 ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal3by3 <- matrix(rep(1,9), ncol = 3) focal11by11 <- matrix(rep(1,121), ncol = 11) r_foc3 <- focal(r, focal3by3, fun = mean, fillNA = TRUE) r_foc11 <- focal(r, focal11by11, fun = mean, fillNA = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-focal2-1.png){#fig-focal2 width=960} ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} - Note how the output raster is smaller as the focal window is larger (edge effect) ::: ## Focal weights (1) - The focal weights we used above were square and evenly weighted ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal3by3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 1 1 [2,] 1 1 1 [3,] 1 1 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal11by11 # same structure, 11×11 ``` ::: ## Focal weights (2) {.smaller} - However, we can also create uneven weights: For example, a [laplacian filter](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace-Filter) is commonly used for edge detection. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} laplacian <- matrix(c(0,1,0,1,-4,1,0,1,0), nrow=3) laplacian ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 0 1 0 [2,] 1 -4 1 [3,] 0 1 0 ``` ::: ::: So are the [sobel filters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobel_operator) — shown on the next slide. ## Focal weights (2) — Sobel {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sobel_x <- matrix(c(-1,-2,-1,0,0,0,1,2,1), nrow=3) sobel_x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] -1 0 1 [2,] -2 0 2 [3,] -1 0 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sobel_y <- matrix(c(1,0,-1,2,0,-2,1,0,-1), nrow=3) sobel_y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 2 1 [2,] 0 0 0 [3,] -1 -2 -1 ``` ::: ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-edgedetection-1.png){#fig-edgedetection width=960} ::: ::: ## Focal Operations = Convolutions {.smaller} A focal operation with a weight matrix *is* a **discrete convolution**: $$(\text{output})_{i,j} = \sum_{m}\sum_{n} w_{m,n} \cdot r_{i+m,\, j+n}$$ This is exactly the operation in **convolutional neural networks (CNNs)**: | Hand-crafted kernel | Equivalent CNN concept | |---------------------|----------------------| | Gaussian blur | Smoothing / anti-aliasing layer | | Sobel x/y | Edge detection layer | | Mean filter | Average pooling | **The key difference**: in deep learning, kernels are *learned from data* rather than designed manually. ::: {.notes} - A CNN is essentially many stacked focal operations with *learned* kernels - The Sobel filter is exactly what a CNN's first conv layer approximates when trained on natural images - Larger kernels → more smoothing = more bias, less variance ::: ## From cells to real world units (1) - We have been specifying our focal weights in terms of cell units - In most cases, it is more reasonable to work with real world units - The resolution of our raster is `0.008333333` (see `res(r)`) and since our raster is in `WGS84`, the units is "degrees". - To work with more managable units, we can convert the raster to a projected CRS that uses "meters", e.g. [EPSG 2169](https://epsg.io/2169) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.008333333 0.008333333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Reproject to a "projected" CRS r_2169 <- project(r, "EPSG:2169") ``` ::: ## From cells to real world units (2) - The resolution of our new raster is 771.9714782 meters. - We can resample this to 1 km to simplify things ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res(r_2169) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 771.9715 771.9715 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # first, create template raster with the same extent and 1km resolution template <- rast(res = 1000, ext = ext(r_2169)) # then, resample to this template r_2169 <- resample(r_2169, template) ``` ::: ## Focal weights with `focalMat` - `focalMat` creates focal matrices in real-world units (CRS units) - Shapes: *circle* (`d` = radius), *rectangle* (`d` = dimensions), *Gauss* (`d` = sigma) - Values sum to 1; matrix size adapts to raster resolution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_circle <- focalMat(x = r_2169, d = 2000, "circle") focal_circle ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 0.00000000 0.09090909 0.00000000 [2,] 0.09090909 0.09090909 0.09090909 [3,] 0.09090909 0.09090909 0.09090909 [4,] 0.09090909 0.09090909 0.09090909 [5,] 0.00000000 0.09090909 0.00000000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Circle filter (2 km radius)](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Focal weights with `focalMat` — Gauss ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gauss <- focalMat(x = r_2169, d = 2000, "Gauss") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gaussian filter (sigma = 2 km)](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Focal functions in terrain processing - Focal functions are used to calculate the slope of a specific location, e.g. using the algorithm by @horn1981 - Similarly, calculating the aspect (azimuth) of a location is a very typical task when dealing with elevation data - These algorithms are used so often, that they are implemented in a dedicated function (`terrain()`) ::: {.notes} - `terrain()` is a convenience wrapper around a focal operation with a specific kernel - Horn's algorithm uses a 3×3 weighted neighborhood to estimate the x/y gradient, from which slope and aspect are derived ::: ## Focal functions in terrain processing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) terrain(r, "slope") |> plot(main = "Slope") terrain(r, "aspect") |> plot(main = "Aspect") par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-terrain-1.png){#fig-terrain width=960} ::: ::: # Raster–Vector Operations {.titlepage} ## Raster–Vector Operations {.smaller} Vector data represents discrete geometries: **points**, **lines**, **polygons** — each with a geometry and attributes. Three fundamental operations linking rasters and vectors: | Operation | Function | What it does | |-----------|----------|-------------| | **Crop** | `crop()` | Reduce raster extent to bounding box of vector | | **Mask** | `mask()` | Set cells outside vector geometry to NA | | **Extract** | `extract()` | Get raster cell values at vector locations | ::: {.notes} - `crop()` + `mask()` almost always used together: crop first (fast — clips extent), then mask (precise — removes cells outside geometry) - `extract()` bridges to tabular analysis — returns a data frame, not a raster ::: ## Crop & Mask ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_muni <- lux[5, ] # one municipality polygon r_crop <- crop(r, one_muni) r_mask <- mask(r_crop, one_muni) ``` ::: ## Crop & Mask ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lesson2_files/figure-revealjs/fig-crop-mask-1.png){#fig-crop-mask width=960} ::: ::: ## Extract {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sample 20 random point locations pts <- spatSample(r, 20, as.points = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) # Elevation value at each point extract(r, pts) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID elevation 1 1 226 2 2 278 3 3 359 4 4 380 5 5 294 ``` ::: ::: `extract()` also accepts polygon geometries and an aggregation function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Mean elevation per municipality polygon extract(r, lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID elevation 1 1 467.1052 2 2 333.8629 3 3 377.3712 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - Polygon extract with `fun =` is similar to `zonal()`, but works on vector geometry directly (no rasterizing) - For large datasets, `rasterize()` + `zonal()` is usually faster - `extract()` without `fun =` returns every cell value per polygon — useful for building classification training data ::: ## Summary | Type | Scope | Key functions | |------|-------|---------------| | **Global** | Entire raster | `global()`, `distance()` | | **Zonal** | Defined regions | `zonal()`, `rasterize()` | | **Local** | Per cell | `classify()`, `>`, `&`, spectral indices | | **Focal** | Moving window | `focal()`, `focalMat()`, `terrain()` | | **Vector ops** | Geometry-based | `crop()`, `mask()`, `extract()` | ## References {#refs}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
